reviews.review:
I'd like to preface this by saying my hours are incorrect as I played most of the time "offline steam" on my steam deck while playing other games for obvious reasons.

I really do want to give this a positive rating and I think possibly in the future it could easily be one.  With that being said I think the incrementality of this game is fundamentally flawed or perhaps they just have ideas that seem unappealing to me personally.  Generally speaking in incremental games you will slowly level, acquire better tools or methods for obtaining resources and such and things tend to flow smoothly, steadily ramping up productions as you yourself level.

Right out the gate the game is frustrating to navigate with the constant skill swapping in order to get resources or tools to do the skill you actually want to train.  Intuitively you might think this is good right? It makes the skills naturally tie into one another.  Sure it does do that, but for a game where you're meant to just set your little man to the task and have him do things automatically, I sure did find myself constantly and annoyingly having to dip back into other skills just to do the skill I wanted for 20 minutes.

My final point of negative was the content gap in relation to xp scaling.  Normally I would attribute this to a game being early access and naturally that would resolve as the game moved towards 1.0 however this game has been officially released as of August.  Once you get to the higher levels of 70-80+ the rate at which you level grinds to a crawl and no new methods of training open up outside of just spamming your inventory with global xp boosting items.  When xp requirements continue to scale to the point where the overwhelming majority of your game time will be those levels, there has to be new training methods opening up as well or the game isn't worth playing past the halfway point.

All of this may seem like I didn't like the game.  I did enjoy it for a time.  I loved the art style and frankly the brutal level scaling reminds me of Runescapes later level scaling, which may have been an influence? Im not sure.  I don't believe it entirely fits for this game unless you're able to add more content as well as increase the players ability to AFK for long periods.  It functions well in a game like Melvor because the player can set an action and close the game while still having your little man do things in the background.

I'd love to see a couple things:

• IF we're keeping global xp items we need multi-crafts to combine them into higher tiers because the inventory clutter is horrific.  On that note we also need more inventory slots.

• Items that give speed increases to skills like potions should have massively increased charges/capacity to take up less space.  If that means you are unable to use multiple at once that is a fair tradeoff.

• Tools need to last significantly longer.  I enjoy macro account planning but I should be able to AFK a skill for a significant time before needing to replace tools, which isn't possible unless you gut your inventory and even then I found it not satisfactory. Perhaps tools as a permanent unlock where you feed crafted/looted tools into it for more charges to eliminate the inventory clutter.

•Larger stack sizes if you're going to keep the inventory smaller.  Frankly both increasing the stack sizes as well as the inventory size is probably the way to go.

•Filling the gaps in content in the higher levels
